claim: An in vivo RNAi screen in Drosophila class IV dendritic arborization (C4da) neurons identified the conserved Ret receptor as an important regulator of dendrite development.
source: We conducted an in vivo RNAi screen in Drosophila class IV dendritic arborization (C4da) neurons and identified the conserved Ret receptor, known to play a role in axon guidance, as an important regulator of dendrite development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental approach described in the abstract and detailed in the results section showing RNAi screening methodology and identification of Ret.

claim: Loss of Ret results in severe dendrite defects due to loss of extracellular matrix adhesion.
source: The loss of Ret results in severe dendrite defects due to loss of extracellular matrix adhesion, thus impairing growth within a 2D plane.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dendrite-ECM detachment in Ret mutants as described in the results and shown in figures.

claim: Ret interacts with integrins to regulate dendrite adhesion via rac1.
source: We provide evidence that Ret interacts with integrins to regulate dendrite adhesion via rac1.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments, genetic interaction studies, and colocalization data presented in the results.

claim: Ret is required for dendrite stability and normal F-actin distribution.
source: In addition, Ret is required for dendrite stability and normal F-actin distribution suggesting it has an essential role in dendrite maintenance.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing increased dendrite turnover and LifeAct imaging showing abnormal F-actin distribution in Ret mutants.

claim: Knockdown of Ret with two independent RNAi lines led to strong dendrite defects in C4da neurons.
source: Using this approach, we screened approximately 400 RNAi lines targeting IgSFs and RTKs and found that knockdown of Ret with two independent lines led to strong dendrite defects in C4da neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi screening and visual evidence in Figure 1A showing dendrite morphology defects.

claim: Ret knockdown resulted in abnormal C4da dendrite patterning with crossing of dendritic branches and incomplete coverage of their receptive field.
source: Knockdown of Ret resulted in abnormal C4da dendrite patterning with crossing of dendritic branches and incomplete coverage of their receptive field.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data and quantitative analysis of dendrite morphology in Ret RNAi animals.

claim: Ret does not cause defects in other classes of da neurons besides C4da neurons.
source: We did not observe defects in other classes of da neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and data not shown) suggesting that Ret plays a specific role in C4da neuron dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by observation of class I da neurons in Ret mutants showing no obvious phenotype.

claim: Drosophila Ret encodes a highly conserved receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) with neuronal expression.
source: Drosophila Ret encodes a highly conserved receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) with neuronal expression (Sugaya et al., 1994; Hahn and Bishop, 2001; Kallijärvi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature characterizing Drosophila Ret.

claim: A Gal4 enhancer trap line inserted within the 5′-region of the Ret gene showed C4da neuron expression.
source: A Gal4 enhancer trap line inserted within the 5′-region of the Ret gene showed C4da neuron expression when driving a GFP reporter (UAS-CD8-GFP, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis using a Gal4 enhancer trap line and visualization with GFP reporter as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ret was detected throughout the dendritic arbor showing almost continuous staining along major dendrites and a more granular pattern in terminal dendrites.
source: Interestingly, Ret was detected throughout the dendritic arbor showing almost continuous staining along major dendrites (Figure 1C,C′) and a more granular pattern in terminal dendrites (Figure 1C,C′′).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis using Ret-specific antibodies as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The strongest Ret puncta consistently localized to the basal side of dendrites facing the ECM.
source: In addition, the strongest Ret puncta consistently localized to the basal side of dendrites facing the ECM (Figure 1C′,C′′).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis with Z-plane reslicing showing Ret localization as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Ret mutant animals, only residual immunoreactivity could be detected in C4da neuron somata but not in dendrites.
source: In Ret mutant animals, only residual immunoreactivity could be detected in C4da neuron somata but not in dendrites (Figure 1E,E′,F) suggesting that the allelic combination used is hypomorphic.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis and quantification of Ret signal in mutant animals as shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: RetC168 mutant animals showed very similar dendrite defects of C4da neurons compared to RNAi results.
source: Compared to our RNAi results, we found very similar dendrite defects of C4da neurons in RetC168 mutant animals (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging comparing RNAi and genetic mutant phenotypes as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dendrite defects in RetC168 mutants were strongly enhanced when combined with a chromosomal deficiency line.
source: These defects were strongly enhanced when we combined RetC168 with a chromosomal deficiency line (Df(2L)Bsc312, Figure 2C), indicating that RetC168 is indeed a hypomorphic allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic analysis comparing RetC168 homozygotes with RetC168/Df trans-heterozygotes as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ret mutant C4da neurons displayed incomplete coverage of the receptive field, with dendritic terminals exhibiting patchy distribution.
source: Strikingly, Ret mutant C4da neurons displayed incomplete coverage of the receptive field, with dendritic terminals exhibiting patchy distribution, reflecting abnormalities in both shape and growth directionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantitative analysis of dendritic field coverage in Ret mutants.

claim: Ret mutant C4da neurons displayed severe isoneuronal dendrite crossing, resulting in extensive overlap of dendritic branches.
source: In addition, we observed severe isoneuronal dendrite crossing, resulting in extensive overlap of dendritic branches not normally observed in controls (Figure 2B,C, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging showing dendrite crossing in Ret mutants as indicated in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Virtually all overlapping dendrites in Ret mutant larvae were not within the same focal plane, but grew in different planes without directly contacting one another.
source: Detailed 3D analysis of dendrite crossing points revealed that virtually all overlapping dendrites were not within the same focal plane, but grew in different planes without directly contacting one another (Figure 2D,D′,D′′).
evidence: The claim is supported by high resolution 3D confocal imaging analysis as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ret mutant C4da neurons did not show a significant reduction in total dendrite length.
source: Despite the severe patterning and field coverage defects, Ret mutant C4da neurons did not show a significant reduction in total dendrite length (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of total dendrite length as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ret mutant C4da neurons displayed excessive crossings of isoneuronal dendrites outside their normal 2D growth plane.
source: They did however display excessive crossings of isoneuronal dendrites outside their normal 2D growth plane (Figure 2F) and significantly reduced dendritic field coverage (see Figure 5B,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of out-of-plane crossing events as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In Ret mutant neurons, large stretches of dendrites, in particular terminal arbors, were detached from the ECM and enclosed by the epidermis.
source: In Ret mutant neurons however, large stretches of dendrites, in particular terminal arbors, were detached from the ECM and enclosed by the epidermis (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by high resolution confocal imaging of dendrites and ECM markers as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Approximately 11% of dendrites were detached from the ECM in Ret mutant C4da neurons within the dorsal field.
source: Ret mutant C4da neurons however displayed frequent detachment and out of plane crossing of dendrites (Figure 3B′,B′′) resulting in approx. 11% ECM-detached dendrites within the dorsal field (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite-ECM interaction as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Trans-heterozygous combinations of Ret and mys or mew integrin alleles resulted in a significant increase in dendrite crossing defects and substantial loss of dendrite-ECM interaction.
source: While animals heterozygous for Ret or integrin mutations showed no significant dendrite detachment compared to wildtype, trans-heterozygous combinations of Ret and mys or mew integrin alleles resulted in a significant increase in dendrite crossing defects (not shown) and a substantial loss of dendrite-ECM interaction (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments and quantitative analysis as shown in Figure 3D-H.

claim: About 10% of dendrites were detached from the ECM in RetC168/mewM6 and Ret C168/mys1 trans-heterozygous animals.
source: Similarly to Ret mutant C4da neurons, about 10% of dendrites were detached from the ECM in RetC168/mewM6 and Ret C168/mys1 trans-heterozygous animals (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite-ECM interaction in trans-heterozygous animals as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ret and integrins act in the same genetic pathway to promote dendrite–matrix interactions.
source: These results suggest that Ret and integrins act in the same genetic pathway to promote dendrite–matrix interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction experiments showing enhancement of dendrite-ECM detachment phenotypes in trans-heterozygous combinations.

claim: Ret showed partial colocalization with Mew or Mys in punctate structures in C4da neuron dendrites.
source: We found partial colocalization of Ret and Mew or Mys in punctate structures in C4da neuron dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of co-expressed Ret and integrins as shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Transfected S2 cells displayed colocalization of Ret and Mys, particularly in filopodia-like structures close to the cell surface.
source: Consistently, transfected S2 cells also displayed colocalization of Ret and Mys, particularly in filopodia-like structures close to the cell surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) suggesting that Ret and integrins may form a molecular complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry in S2 cells as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ret showed strong and specific interaction with Mys in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Indeed, Ret showed strong and specific interaction with Mys, and additional co-expression of Mew robustly increased the Ret-integrin interaction indicating that Ret preferentially interacts with the mature integrin complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in S2 cells as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ret displayed pronounced surface labeling along the entire dendritic tree.
source: Ret itself displayed pronounced surface labeling along the entire dendritic tree, strongly indicating that Ret is present at the cell surface of C4da neurons (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell surface immunostaining of pHluorin-tagged Ret as shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Ret showed significant colocalization with Mew in dendrites.
source: Strikingly, Ret showed significant colocalization with Mew in dendrites (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell surface immunostaining and colocalization analysis as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Many of the high intensity peaks of Mew showed concomitant Ret signal peaks indicating that Mew and Ret can be colocalized in dendrites and at the surface of C4da neurons.
source: In particular, many of the high intensity peaks of Mew showed concomitant Ret signal peaks with both tags indicating that Mew and Ret can be indeed colocalized in dendrites and at the surface of C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by intensity plot analysis of Ret and Mew signals along dendrites as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Quantitative colocalization analysis of Ret and integrin signals in C4da neuron somata and dendrites revealed a strong positive correlation based on Pearson coefficient analysis.
source: Quantitative colocalization analysis of Ret and integrin signals in C4da neuron somata and dendrites revealed a strong positive correlation based on Pearson coefficient analysis for overexpressed Ret/Mew and Ret/Mys (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Endogenous Ret displayed a significant degree of co-distribution with Mys and Mew in C4da neurons.
source: Finally, we assessed colocalization of endogenous Ret with overexpressed integrins. As for Ret overexpression, endogenous Ret displayed a significant degree of co-distribution with Mys and Mew in C4da neurons (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of endogenous Ret with overexpressed integrins as shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The majority of colocalized Ret and integrin signals were found facing the basal dendritic surface which contacts the ECM.
source: Interestingly, the majority of colocalized signals were found facing the basal dendritic surface which contacts the ECM (Figure 4D′,E′, arrows and Video 1) suggesting that Ret and integrins are potentially interacting at adhesion sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by Z-plane analysis of colocalization showing basal localization as shown in Figure 4D' and 4E'.

claim: Driving expression of Ret in C4da neurons was sufficient to completely rescue the dendrite growth and crossing phenotype in Ret mutant background.
source: Indeed, driving expression of Ret in C4da neurons was sufficient to completely rescue the dendrite growth and crossing phenotype (Figure 5B,B′ and Figure 5C,C′) demonstrating that Ret is cell-autonomously required for C4da dendrite patterning.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments expressing Ret-mCherry in C4da neurons as shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Overexpression of Mys and Mew in Ret mutant C4da neurons completely prevented dendritic out of plane crossing indicating restored interaction with the ECM.
source: Although the overexpression of integrins did not rescue all aspects of the Ret dendritic growth phenotype (Figure 5D,D′), it completely prevented dendritic out of plane crossing indicating restored interaction with the ECM (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments overexpressing integrins in Ret mutant C4da neurons as shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Integrin overexpression in C4da neurons did not rescue coverage defects of the dendritic field in Ret mutant animals.
source: However, unlike Ret itself, integrin overexpression in C4da neurons did not rescue coverage defects of the dendritic field in Ret mutant animals (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendritic field coverage in rescue experiments as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Integrin overexpression was able to completely suppress Ret dependent photoreceptor degeneration in the compound eye.
source: Integrin overexpression itself did not cause any eye phenotype, but was able to completely suppress Ret dependent photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of eye phenotypes in flies overexpressing Ret with or without integrins as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of rac1 function led to strong dendrite-ECM detachment and epithelial enclosure of dendrites highly similar to Ret and integrin mutant phenotypes.
source: Using loss of function analysis, we tested whether rac1 is involved in dendrite-ECM adhesion of C4da neurons. Loss of rac1 function led to strong dendrite-ECM detachment and epithelial enclosure of dendrites highly similar to Ret and integrin mutant phenotypes (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of dendrite-ECM interaction in rac1 mutants as shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: In rac1 mutant C4da neurons, 15% of dendrites in the field were detached from the ECM.
source: Overall, in rac1 mutant C4da neurons, 15% of dendrites in the field were detached from the ECM, an effect that was even more pronounced when the gene dosage of the other two rac-like GTPases, rac2, and mtl was also reduced (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite-ECM detachment in rac1 mutants as shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Loss of rac1 function led to many non-contacting crossing defects of dendritic branches indicating that self-avoidance is impaired due to 3D growth of dendrites.
source: In both cases, loss of rac1 function also led to many non-contacting crossing defects of dendritic branches (Figure 6B,C arrows, and Figure 6E) indicating that self-avoidance is impaired due to 3D growth of dendrites lacking rac1 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of dendrite crossing in rac1 mutants as shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and 6E.

claim: When combining rac1 alleles with Ret or integrin mutant alleles, strong enhancement of dendritic loss of ECM adhesion was observed.
source: When combining rac1 alleles with Ret or integrin mutant alleles however, we observed strong enhancement of dendritic loss of ECM adhesion (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments as shown in Figure 6J-L.

claim: For both Ret/rac1 and integrin/rac1 heteroallelic combinations, 15–20% percent of dendrites lost contact with the ECM.
source: For both Ret/rac1 and integrin/rac1 heteroallelic combinations, 15–20% percent of dendrites lost contact with the ECM indicating strong crosstalk and regulation of Ret and integrins via rac1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite-ECM detachment in trans-heterozygous combinations as shown in Figure 6M.

claim: rac1 functions in the same pathway as Ret and integrins in regulating the attachment of dendrites to the ECM.
source: These findings strongly suggest that rac1 functions in the same pathway as Ret and integrins in regulating the attachment of dendrites to the ECM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction experiments showing enhancement of dendrite-ECM detachment phenotypes.

claim: Neither integrin nor rac1 loss of function resulted in major defects in dendrite growth and coverage of C4da neurons.
source: Unlike Ret, neither integrin nor rac1 loss of function resulted in major defects in dendrite growth and coverage of C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes across different mutants showing that coverage defects are specific to Ret.

claim: In wildtype C4da neurons, significant turnover of terminal dendrites could be observed during late larval development.
source: In wildtype C4da neurons, significant turnover of terminal dendrites could be observed (Figure 7A), as reported previously (Parrish et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data as shown in Figure 7A and cited previous literature.

claim: Analysis of dendrite turnover between 72 and 96 hr AEL revealed highly increased dynamics of dendritic growth and retraction in Ret mutant C4da neurons, with major remodeling of the terminal dendrite arbors.
source: Remarkably, analysis of dendrite turnover between 72 and 96 hr AEL revealed highly increased dynamics of dendritic growth and retraction, with major remodeling of the terminal dendrite arbors.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging and quantitative analysis of dendrite dynamics in Ret mutants.

claim: Both growth and retraction of dendrite terminals in Ret mutant C4da neurons were increased two to threefold compared to wildtype.
source: Both growth and retraction of dendrite terminals in Ret mutant C4da neurons were increased two to threefold compared to wildtype (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite growth and retraction as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The growth/retraction ratio of dendrites was significantly reduced in Ret mutant C4da neurons due to a disproportional increase in retraction compared to growth.
source: Overall, the growth/retraction ratio of dendrites was significantly reduced in Ret mutant C4da neurons due to a disproportional increase in retraction compared to growth (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of growth/retraction ratios as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Wildtype C4da neurons displayed fairly even distribution of F-actin along major dendrites, while terminal branches typically featured hotspots of increased F-actin levels.
source: Wildtype C4da neurons displayed fairly even distribution of F-actin along major dendrites, while terminal branches typically featured hotspots of increased F-actin levels (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by LifeAct imaging in wildtype C4da neurons as shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: F-actin levels were significantly increased and unevenly distributed in proximal regions of primary dendrites of Ret mutant neurons.
source: In contrast, F-actin levels were significantly increased and unevenly distributed in proximal regions of primary dendrites of Ret mutant neurons (Figure 7E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by LifeAct imaging and quantitative analysis in Ret mutant C4da neurons as shown in Figure 7E and 7G.

claim: Aberrantly crossing terminal branches in Ret mutants had increased levels of F-actin, while other terminals displayed either normal or very low F-actin levels compared to wildtype.
source: Strikingly, aberrantly crossing terminal branches had increased levels of F-actin, while other terminals displayed either normal or very low F-actin levels compared to wildtype (Figure 7G, arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by LifeAct imaging showing differential F-actin distribution in Ret mutant dendrites as shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Ret is required for the appropriate localization of F-actin in dendrites, which likely contributes to the destabilization of growing branches.
source: These data clearly show that Ret is required for the appropriate localization of F-actin in dendrites, which likely contributes to the destabilization of growing branches.
evidence: The claim is inferred from LifeAct imaging data showing abnormal F-actin distribution in Ret mutants.

claim: Loss of Ret function impairs dendrite stability and increases dynamic growth and retraction of dendritic branches resulting in the failure of complete receptive field coverage.
source: Taken together, our findings show that loss of Ret function impairs dendrite stability and increases dynamic growth and retraction of dendritic branches resulting in the failure of complete receptive field coverage.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental observations including time-lapse imaging and field coverage analysis.

claim: Ret is a conserved receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) expressed in the nervous system of vertebrates and D. melanogaster.
source: Ret is a conserved receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) expressed in the nervous system of vertebrates (Pachnis et al., 1993; Schuchardt et al., 1994) and D. melanogaster (Sugaya et al., 1994; Hahn and Bishop, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature characterizing Ret expression.

claim: Ret regulates motor neuron axon guidance.
source: it regulates motor neuron axon guidance (Kramer et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ret regulates dopaminergic neuron maintenance and regeneration.
source: dopaminergic neuron maintenance and regeneration (Kowsky et al., 2007; Kramer et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ret regulates mechanoreceptor differentiation and projection to the spinal cord and medulla.
source: and mechanoreceptor differentiation and projection to the spinal cord and medulla (Bourane et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ret signaling is activated by binding to glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family ligands and their high affinity co-receptors, the GDNF family receptors (GFRα).
source: Ret signaling is activated by binding to glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family ligands and their high affinity co-receptors, the GDNF family receptors (GFRα) (reviewed in Runeberg-Roos and Saarma, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Loss of function mutations of Ret lead to Hirschprung's disease displaying colonic aganglionosis due to defective enteric nervous system development.
source: Ret also plays an important role in human development and disease as loss of function mutations of Ret lead to Hirschprung's disease displaying colonic aganglionosis due to defective enteric nervous system development (Amiel et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on human disease.

claim: Ret gain of function mutations are causal for autosomal dominant MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2) type medullary thyroid carcinoma.
source: Conversely, Ret gain of function mutations are causal for autosomal dominant MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2) type medullary thyroid carcinoma (Lairmore et al., 1993; Almeida and Hoff, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on human disease.

claim: Prior to this study, Ret has not been implicated in dendrite development.
source: Prior to this study, Ret has not been implicated in dendrite development.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the findings based on literature review.

claim: Ret is required specifically for 2D growth of C4da neurons by regulating integrin dependent dendrite-ECM adhesion.
source: Here, we show that Ret is required specifically for 2D growth of C4da neurons by regulating integrin dependent dendrite-ECM adhesion.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: C4da neuron dendrites are normally virtually always in contact with the ECM and the basal surface of the epithelium lining the larval cuticle, and thus tightly sandwiched between the two compartments.
source: Normally, C4da neuron dendrites are virtually always in contact with the ECM and the basal surface of the epithelium lining the larval cuticle, and thus tightly sandwiched between the two compartments (Yamamoto et al., 2006; Han et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing C4da neuron dendrite positioning.

claim: In both integrin and Ret mutants, dendrite-ECM adhesion is impaired.
source: In both integrin and Ret mutants, dendrite-ECM adhesion is impaired.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dendrite-ECM detachment in both mutant types.

claim: Ret and integrins can co-localize in dendrites and thus likely form a functional complex that could induce and maintain adhesion of dendrites to the ECM.
source: Ret and integrins can co-localize in dendrites and thus likely form a functional complex that could induce and maintain adhesion of dendrites to the ECM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from colocalization and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Ret loss of function primarily leads to detached terminal dendrite branches.
source: Since Ret loss of function primarily leads to detached terminal dendrite branches, it is tempting to speculate that Ret might be required to recruit integrins to sites of growing dendrites to promote ECM interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing preferential detachment of terminal branches in Ret mutants.

claim: Vertebrate Ret has been shown to cooperate with Ephrins to ensure high fidelity axon guidance in motor neurons by mediating attractive EphrinA reverse signaling.
source: Interestingly, vertebrate Ret has been shown to cooperate with Ephrins to ensure high fidelity axon guidance in motor neurons by mediating attractive EphrinA reverse signaling (Kramer et al., 2006; Bonanomi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Ret function in axon guidance.

claim: Dscam and Netrin-Frazzled signaling act in parallel in class III da neurons.
source: So far, only parallel receptor pathways like Dscam and Netrin-Frazzled signaling in class III da neurons (Matthews and Grueber, 2011) or Dscam/integrins (Han et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012) have been identified co-regulating dendrite morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Integrins have been shown to display extensive crosstalk with other signaling receptors, including RTKs.
source: Integrins have been shown to display extensive crosstalk with other signaling receptors, including RTKs (Ivaska and Heino, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Matrix-bound VEGF can induce complex formation between VEGFR2 and β1-integrin with concomitant targeting of β1-integrin to focal adhesions in endothelial cells.
source: For example, matrix-bound VEGF can induce complex formation between VEGFR2 and β1-integrin with concomitant targeting of β1-integrin to focal adhesions in endothelial cells (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature providing an example of RTK-integrin crosstalk.

claim: Ret can enhance integrin mediated adhesion in vitro.
source: Previous studies provide evidence for Ret-integrin-Rac1 interplay in vitro showing that Ret can enhance integrin mediated adhesion (Cockburn et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Ret function in cell culture.

claim: Ret can induce Rac1 dependent lamellipodia formation in cell culture models.
source: and induce Rac1 dependent lamellipodia formation (Fukuda et al., 2002) in cell culture models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Ret function in cell culture.

claim: Rac1 is involved in neurite outgrowth on the integrin substrates laminin and fibronectin in primary chick motor neurons.
source: In primary chick motor neurons, Rac1 is involved in neurite outgrowth on the integrin substrates laminin and fibronectin (Kuhn et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Rac1 has previously been shown to regulate dendrite branching in C4da neurons.
source: Interestingly, Rac1 has previously been shown to regulate dendrite branching in C4da neurons (Lee et al., 2003; Emoto et al., 2004), however a role in dendrite adhesion in vivo has not been described before.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Rac1 function in C4da neurons.

claim: MAPK, Src and PI3K can be activated by constitutively active Ret overexpression in the Drosophila compound eye.
source: In Drosophila, MAPK, Src and PI3K can be activated by constitutively active Ret overexpression in the compound eye (Read et al., 2005; Dar et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Ret signaling in Drosophila.

claim: Novel inhibitors of Ret signaling targeting Raf, Src, and S6-Kinase (S6K) prevent lethality induced by Ret over-activation in a Drosophila multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2) model.
source: Moreover, novel inhibitors of Ret signaling targeting Raf, Src, and S6-Kinase (S6K) prevent lethality induced by Ret over-activation in a Drosophila multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2) model (Dar et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Ret signaling in Drosophila disease models.

claim: S6K has been shown to be involved in dendrite growth but not tiling in C4da neurons.
source: Interestingly, S6K has been shown to be involved in dendrite growth but not tiling in C4da neurons (Koike-Kumagai et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on S6K function in C4da neurons.

claim: Drosophila Ret is a highly conserved molecule, but its cognate vertebrate ligand GDNF is not.
source: Drosophila Ret is a highly conserved molecule, its cognate vertebrate ligand GDNF, however is not (Airaksinen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Ret ligand conservation.

claim: Drosophila Ret can neither bind GDNF nor transduce GDNF signaling, although it has been shown to contain a functional tyrosine kinase domain.
source: In addition, Drosophila Ret can neither bind GDNF nor transduce GDNF signaling, although it has been shown to contain a functional tyrosine kinase domain (Abrescia et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Drosophila Ret biochemistry.

claim: A Drosophila GFR-like homolog (dGFRL) has recently been characterized and was found to function and interact with the NCAM homolog FasII.
source: A Drosophila GFR-like homolog (dGFRL) has recently been characterized and was found to function and interact with the NCAM homolog FasII (Kallijärvi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Drosophila GFR homolog.

claim: Ret's functional interaction partners in dendrite development differ significantly from the previously described co-factors in other systems.
source: Therefore, it appears that Ret's functional interaction partners in dendrite development differ significantly from the previously described co-factors in other systems.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of Ret ligands and co-receptors in Drosophila versus vertebrates.

claim: Ret plays a role in the maintenance of dopaminergic neurons and motor axon growth in mouse.
source: due to its role in the maintenance of dopaminergic neurons and motor axon growth in mouse (Kramer et al., 2006, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on mammalian Ret function.

claim: The formation of dorsal root ganglia derived mechanosensory neurons and their afferent and efferent fiber growth and innervation depends on Ret expression.
source: Moreover, the formation of a dorsal root ganglia derived mechanosensory neurons and their afferent and efferent fiber growth and innervation depends on Ret expression (Bourane et al., 2009; Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Ret function in sensory neurons.

claim: Ret has a novel role in dendrite branch growth and stability in Drosophila C4da neurons.
source: In summary, we describe a novel role for the Ret receptor in dendrite branch growth and stability in Drosophila C4da neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the main findings supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: Ret has cell-autonomous effects on ECM adhesion and F-actin localization in C4da neurons.
source: This role involves cell-autonomous effects of Ret on ECM adhesion, and F-actin localization in these neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments and imaging data showing cell-autonomous function.

claim: Dendritic adhesion defects attributable to Ret are linked to integrin and rac1 function featuring a novel and possibly conserved mode of action for Ret in dendrite development.
source: Moreover, we have linked dendritic adhesion defects attributable to Ret to integrin and rac1 function featuring a novel and possibly conserved mode of action for Ret in dendrite development.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by genetic and biochemical interaction data.
